title: Ottoman Iraq: the Three Provinces
subtitle: 1534–1831 · Baghdad, Basra and Mosul on the Persian Frontier — the Wars over Baghdad, the Mamluk Pashas, the Conversion of the Tribes to Shiism, and the Shrine Cities as a State Within a State

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The Ottoman settlement of the three provinces, the Persian interlude and Murad IV's reconquest, the localised garrison and the rise of the pashas, Hasan and Ahmad Pasha and Nadir Shah's sieges, the Mamluk household as a dynasty, Sulayman the Great, Dawud Pasha and the end, and the tribal and Kurdish powers

entries.group: The Governors and Pashas of Baghdad
entries.label: The Ottoman settlement of the three provinces
entries.hint: Suleiman organised his conquest as three provinces — Baghdad, Basra and Mosul, with Shahrizor in the Kurdish hills — held mainly for defence against Persia. Istanbul kept a janissary garrison and sent governors on short terms, but never applied the land-grant system it used in the Balkans; Iraq was a remittance province, tax-farmed and lightly held. Within a lifetime the garrison had gone native and the governors were losing their grip.
entries.note: Colin Imber, 'The Ottoman Empire, 1300–1650' (2002); Dina Rizk Khoury, 'State and Provincial Society in the Ottoman Empire: Mosul, 1540–1834' (1997).

entries.group: The Governors and Pashas of Baghdad
entries.label: The Persian interlude and Murad IV's reconquest
entries.hint: Shah Abbas took Baghdad in 1623 and put its Sunnis to the sword. Fifteen years later Sultan Murad IV came in person, besieged the city for six weeks, stormed it on Christmas Day 1638, and massacred the garrison and much of the Shia population in turn. The Treaty of Zuhab in 1639 drew a line between the two empires that has barely moved since — and left Iraq on the Ottoman side for good.
entries.note: Rudi Matthee, 'Persia in Crisis' (2012); the Treaty of Zuhab (Qasr-e Shirin), 17 May 1639.

entries.group: The Governors and Pashas of Baghdad
entries.label: The localised garrison and the drift from Istanbul
entries.hint: Through the later seventeenth century the janissaries of Baghdad became a hereditary local corps with property and families, the city's notables — the ayan — grew into a power, and governors came and went too fast to build anything. Real authority pooled at the provincial level. Istanbul still appointed the pasha, but increasingly it appointed whoever already held Baghdad.
entries.note: Tom Nieuwenhuis, 'Politics and Society in Early Modern Iraq' (1982); Thabit Abdullah, 'Merchants, Mamluks, and Murder' (2001).

entries.group: The Governors and Pashas of Baghdad
entries.label: Hasan Pasha, Ahmad Pasha, and Nadir Shah's sieges
entries.hint: Hasan Pasha, sent from Istanbul in 1704, governed for nineteen years and built up a household of Georgian slave-soldiers to serve him. His son Ahmad Pasha inherited both the post and the household. Together they held Baghdad through the terrifying sieges of Nadir Shah — relieved in 1733 after a battle at Samarra, and again in 1743 — and, when Ahmad died in 1747, the household he had built took the government for itself.
entries.note: Michael Axworthy, 'The Sword of Persia: Nader Shah' (2006); Tom Nieuwenhuis (1982).

entries.group: The Governors and Pashas of Baghdad
entries.label: The Mamluk pashas of Baghdad
entries.hint: For eighty years Baghdad was ruled by its own slave-soldier caste — Georgian and Circassian boys bought, converted, trained in the pasha's household, married into it, and promoted. The pasha was chosen from among them, confirmed after the fact by a firman from Istanbul, and paid a tribute. It was a de facto dynasty, of the same kind as the Qaramanli of Tripoli and the Mamluk beys of Egypt — an Ottoman province run by Ottoman methods against Ottoman control.
entries.note: Tom Nieuwenhuis, 'Politics and Society in Early Modern Iraq: Mamluk Pashas, Tribal Shaykhs and Local Rule between 1802 and 1831' (1982).

entries.group: The Governors and Pashas of Baghdad
entries.label: Sulayman the Great
entries.hint: Büyük Süleyman Pasha ruled for twenty-two years, the peak of the Mamluk regime: he broke the Muntafiq's grip on the south, made the desert roads passable, restored order and some prosperity, dealt on his own account with the British, the Persians and the Wahhabis, and kept Istanbul at a comfortable distance. Under him Baghdad recovered toward a hundred thousand people. He died in 1802, the year the Wahhabis sacked Karbala.
entries.note: Tom Nieuwenhuis (1982); ʿAbbas al-ʿAzzawi, 'Ta'rīkh al-ʿIrāq bayn Iḥtilālayn' (1935–56).

entries.group: The Governors and Pashas of Baghdad
entries.label: Dawud Pasha and the end of the regime
entries.hint: The last Mamluk pasha was also the most ambitious: Dawud raised a European-drilled regular army, opened an arsenal and a printing press, and behaved like a sovereign. Mahmud II, done with autonomous provinces, sent Ali Riza Pasha to remove him. Then the plague and the Tigris flood of 1831 killed perhaps half of Baghdad and dissolved Dawud's army; he surrendered, and the Ottomans ruled Iraq directly again for the first time in a century.
entries.note: ʿUthman ibn Sanad al-Baṣri, 'Maṭāliʿ al-Suʿūd bi-Ṭīb Akhbār al-Wālī Dāwūd'; Ebubekir Ceylan, 'The Ottoman Origins of Modern Iraq' (2011).

entries.label: The Muntafiq, the Baban and the Bedouin
entries.hint: Most of Iraq belonged to its own powers. The Muntafiq confederation of the lower Euphrates, led by the sharifian Sa'dun family, was often stronger than the pasha in the south. The Kurdish emirs of Baban, who founded Sulaymaniyya in 1784, played Istanbul and Tehran against each other in the north. And the great Bedouin confederations — the Shammar pushing up from Najd, the Anaza, the Ubayd, the Zubayd — held the desert and taxed the caravans.
entries.note: ʿAbbas al-ʿAzzawi, 'ʿAshāʾir al-ʿIrāq' (1937); Faleh A. Jabar, 'The Sha'irs of Iraq' background in his tribal studies.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The four bloody changes of hands at Baghdad and the Treaty of Zuhab, Nadir Shah's invasions, the Mamluk civil wars and the endless tribal risings, the Wahhabi sack of Karbala, the Baban wars in the Kurdish north, and the fall of Dawud Pasha in the plague and flood of 1831

entries.label: Four changes of hands and the Treaty of Zuhab
entries.hint: Baghdad changed empires four times in a century — Ottoman 1534, still contested, Safavid 1623, Ottoman 1638 — and each capture brought a sectarian massacre, Sunnis under the Persians, Shia and the garrison under Murad IV. The Treaty of Zuhab in 1639 finally fixed the border and ended the contest. The wars had cost the country its last chance to recover on Iranian terms, and welded it to the Ottoman world.
entries.note: Rhoads Murphey, 'Ottoman Warfare 1500–1700' (1999); Rudi Matthee, 'The Politics of Trade in Safavid Iran' (1999).

entries.label: Nadir Shah's invasions
entries.hint: Nadir Shah, the last great Persian conqueror, twice tried to take Iraq — besieging Baghdad in 1733, defeated at Samarra by an Ottoman relief army, and returning in 1743 to besiege Baghdad and Basra again. He also convened a congress of Sunni and Shia scholars at Najaf in 1743 to try to end the schism by recognising Shi'ism as a fifth Sunni school. Both projects failed, and the Treaty of Kerden in 1746 restored the Zuhab line.
entries.note: Michael Axworthy, 'The Sword of Persia: Nader Shah' (2006); Ernest Tucker, 'Nadir Shah's Quest for Legitimacy' (2006).

entries.label: The Mamluk civil wars and the tribal risings
entries.hint: The Mamluk regime fought itself and its subjects continuously. Pashas were assassinated by their rivals, Baghdad was besieged by mamluk factions, and every year brought a campaign against the Muntafiq of the south, the Khaza'il of the mid-Euphrates, the Ka'b of the Shatt, or the Kurds. Holding the country was a permanent low-grade war, and the pasha's real reach usually stopped a day's ride from the city walls.
entries.note: Tom Nieuwenhuis, 'Politics and Society in Early Modern Iraq' (1982); Thabit Abdullah, 'Merchants, Mamluks, and Murder' (2001).

entries.label: The Wahhabi sack of Karbala
entries.hint: On a spring day in 1802 a Najdi army led by Saud ibn Abd al-Aziz stormed Karbala while many of its men were away on pilgrimage, killed thousands in the streets and the shrine, and carried off the treasury of the tomb of Husayn — for the Wahhabis, an idol-house. The pasha's forces did nothing. The massacre hardened Shia identity around the shrines and drew the Ottomans into a long war with the first Saudi state.
entries.note: the Wahhabi chronicle of Ibn Bishr, 'ʿUnwān al-Majd'; Juan Cole, 'Sacred Space and Holy War' (2002).

entries.label: The Baban wars and the Kurdish frontier
entries.hint: The Baban emirs of the Kurdish highlands ran a hereditary principality that owed loyalty to whichever of the two empires was closer or more dangerous. They founded Sulaymaniyya as their seat in 1784, fought the Ottoman governors of Baghdad and Mosul repeatedly, and shifted to Persian protection when it suited — keeping the Ottoman–Persian frontier in Kurdistan in permanent motion and the mountains effectively outside either state.
entries.note: 'Abbas al-'Azzawi, 'Ta'rīkh al-'Irāq' (1935–56); Hakan Özoğlu, 'Kurdish Notables and the Ottoman State' (2004).

entries.label: The fall of Dawud Pasha
entries.hint: Mahmud II sent Ali Riza Pasha to take Baghdad from Dawud. Before the armies could decide it, plague swept the city in the spring of 1831 and the Tigris broke its banks in April, drowning whole quarters. Contemporaries reckoned the population fell by more than half. Dawud's regular army melted, his treasury was underwater, and he surrendered in September. The Mamluk regime, and the long era of indirect rule, were over.
entries.note: ʿUthman ibn Sanad, 'Maṭāliʿ al-Suʿūd'; Ebubekir Ceylan, 'The Ottoman Origins of Modern Iraq' (2011).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The three frontier provinces and their tax-farms, the Mamluk household as a self-perpetuating state, the multezim and the ruin of the land, the hereditary Kurdish and Arab autonomies, the millet communities, and the shrine cities as a state within the state

entries.label: Three provinces, tax-farmed and lightly held
entries.hint: Iraq was governed as a set of remittance provinces — Baghdad, Basra, Mosul, Shahrizor — where Istanbul asked for a fixed yearly payment and a garrison against Persia and little else. The land was not granted to cavalrymen as in the core Ottoman lands but auctioned to tax-farmers. The state's presence outside the walled towns was a tax demand and an occasional punitive column.
entries.note: Dina Rizk Khoury, 'State and Provincial Society in the Ottoman Empire: Mosul, 1540–1834' (1997).

entries.label: The Mamluk household as a state
entries.hint: The Georgian slave-soldier household that Hasan Pasha founded became the government. Boys were bought young, converted, schooled in the pasha's palace, married to his kinswomen, and moved up through the offices of the divan; the ablest of them became pasha in turn. It was a self-recruiting, self-perpetuating ruling caste, loyal to the household rather than to Istanbul — an Ottoman institution turned against Ottoman control.
entries.note: Tom Nieuwenhuis, 'Politics and Society in Early Modern Iraq' (1982); Hala Fattah, 'The Politics of Regional Trade in Iraq, Arabia, and the Gulf' (1997).

entries.label: The tax-farmer and the ruin of the land
entries.hint: In the countryside the real authority was the multezim, the man who had bought the right to collect a district's taxes. Leases were short, so he took the maximum this year and spent nothing on the dikes; when the malikane, the life-lease, made tax-farms into heritable property, it fixed the extractive relationship in place. Whatever irrigation had survived the medieval collapse decayed further under this system.
entries.note: Ariel Salzmann, 'An Ancien Régime Revisited' (Politics & Society, 1993), on Ottoman tax-farm privatization; Dina Rizk Khoury (1997).

entries.label: The hereditary Kurdish and Arab lordships
entries.hint: The Ottomans governed the margins by recognising the lords who were already there. The Kurdish emirates — Baban, Soran, Bahdinan — were 'governed districts', hereditary and self-ruling, providing troops and tribute in theory and doing as they pleased in practice. The Arab tribal confederations were handled the same way: the shaykh was confirmed, given a title and a tax quota, and left to run his people.
entries.note: Hakan Özoğlu, 'Kurdish Notables and the Ottoman State' (2004); Martin van Bruinessen, 'Agha, Shaikh and State' (1992).

entries.label: The millet order and the minorities
entries.hint: Non-Muslims lived under their own communal heads and law: the Jews of Baghdad under a nasi and, later, a chief rabbi recognised by the state; the Christians split among Chaldean Catholics, the Church of the East, Armenians and Syriacs; the Mandaeans of the rivers as a tolerated 'People of the Book'. They paid the poll tax and the usual disabilities, and were mostly left to themselves.
entries.note: Zvi Yehuda, 'The New Babylonian Diaspora' (2017); the Ottoman millet literature in Bruce Masters, 'Christians and Jews in the Ottoman Arab World' (2001).

entries.label: The shrine cities as a state within the state
entries.hint: Najaf and Karbala ran themselves. The Ottoman writ barely reached them; real power lay with the senior mujtahids, the shrine custodians, the neighbourhood gangs that fought over the pilgrim trade, and a Persian consul with money to spend. The endowments, the treasuries and the corpse-tax were theirs. A Shia enclave, governed by its own clergy and toughs, sat inside a Sunni province and answered to no one much.
entries.note: Yitzhak Nakash, 'The Shiʿis of Iraq' (1994); Meir Litvak, 'Shiʿi Scholars of Nineteenth-Century Iraq' (1998).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The conversion of the southern tribes to Shiism, the triumph of Usulism and the birth of the marjaiyya, the shrine cities as the Shia holy land at its height, the Sunni orders and the Khalidi Naqshbandi revival, the Wahhabi shock, and the Jews of Baghdad

entries.label: The southern tribes turn Shia
entries.hint: As the Bedouin of the lower Euphrates settled to grow rice and dates through the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, preachers from Najaf and Karbala converted them, tribe by tribe. A country that had been nominally Sunni or barely Muslim in its tribal south became solidly Twelver Shia. It is the largest change in Iraq's religious make-up since the Arab conquest, and it made the modern Shia majority.
entries.note: Yitzhak Nakash, 'The Conversion of Iraq's Tribes to Shiism' (IJMES 1994) and 'The Shiʿis of Iraq' (1994).

entries.label: The triumph of Usulism and the marjaiyya
entries.hint: At Karbala, Muhammad Baqir Bihbahani defeated the Akhbari school, which had denied the living jurist any special authority, and established the Usuli position: every believer who is not himself a jurist must follow a living mujtahid in all matters of religious practice. From this grew the ranking of scholars, the office of the marjaʿ al-taqlīd, and the clergy's financial independence through the religious tithe. The institutional basis of clerical power was laid here.
entries.note: Juan Cole, 'Shiʿi Clerics in Iraq and Iran, 1722–1780' (1985); Meir Litvak, 'Shiʿi Scholars of Nineteenth-Century Iraq' (1998).

entries.label: The atabat at their height
entries.hint: Najaf, Karbala, Kazimayn and Samarra together were the undisputed centre of the Twelver world: the seminaries where the jurists were trained, the shrines that drew pilgrims and the dead from Iran, India, Lebanon and the Gulf, the great cemetery at Wadi al-Salam. Persian, Indian and local money flowed in as endowments and offerings. For the Shia everywhere, the road to learning and to holiness ran through Iraq.
entries.note: Yitzhak Nakash, 'The Shiʿis of Iraq' (1994); Juan Cole, 'Sacred Space and Holy War' (2002).

entries.label: The Kaylanis and the Khalidi Naqshbandi revival
entries.hint: Sunni religious life ran through the orders and the shrines. The Kaylani family, hereditary keepers of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani's tomb, were a power in Baghdad in their own right. And in the 1810s Khalid al-Baghdadi refounded the Naqshbandi order on a strict, activist, sharia-minded basis; his Khalidiyya spread from Baghdad across Kurdistan, Anatolia and the Arab lands and became the most influential Sufi movement of the late Ottoman century.
entries.note: Butrus Abu-Manneh, 'The Naqshbandiyya-Mujaddidiyya in the Ottoman Lands in the Early 19th Century' (1982); Itzchak Weismann, 'The Naqshbandiyya' (2007).

entries.label: The Wahhabi challenge to the shrines
entries.hint: The Najdi movement's core teaching — that visiting graves and seeking a saint's help is idolatry — struck at both the Shia atabat and the Sunni Sufi shrines. Its raids on Karbala and Najaf, and its capture of Mecca and Medina, were a shock felt across the Muslim world. In Iraq it hardened Shia devotion around the very shrines it attacked, and pushed the Ottoman state toward a self-conscious defence of shrine-centred orthodoxy.
entries.note: Michael Cook, 'On the Origins of Wahhābism' (1992); Alexei Vassiliev, 'The History of Saudi Arabia' (2000).

entries.label: The Jews of Baghdad
entries.hint: Baghdad held one of the great Jewish communities of the Ottoman east — tens of thousands, dominant in the city's trade and finance, with its own courts and schools and a continuous line of scholars. The tombs of Ezekiel at Kifl and of Ezra on the lower Tigris drew Jewish pilgrims. It was a community entering its golden age just before Dawud Pasha's exactions sent its merchants abroad and began the diaspora that would carry the name Baghdadi across Asia.
entries.note: Zvi Yehuda, 'The New Babylonian Diaspora' (2017); Nissim Rejwan, 'The Jews of Iraq' (1985).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The local chronicle tradition, poetry between Turkish, Persian and Arabic and the Iraqi maqam, the building of the Mamluk pashas and the gilding of the shrines, Dawud Pasha's press, and the last Mandaean scribes

entries.label: The local chronicle tradition
entries.hint: Iraq kept a modest but unbroken habit of writing its own history. Murtada Nazmizade compiled a chronicle of Baghdad and its rulers in the 1720s; a century later Uthman ibn Sanad al-Basri wrote a detailed panegyric history of Dawud Pasha's reign, and Ibrahim Fasih al-Haydari carried the record on. The shrine cities produced their own biographical dictionaries of scholars. It is the raw material from which the period is reconstructed.
entries.note: Murtaḍā Nazmīzāde, 'Gulshan-i Khulafā'; ʿUthman ibn Sanad, 'Maṭāliʿ al-Suʿūd'; the survey in Ebubekir Ceylan (2011).

entries.label: Poetry between three languages and the Iraqi maqam
entries.hint: Educated Iraq wrote in three registers — Ottoman Turkish for the divan and the officials, Persian for the shrine cities and the cultivated, Arabic for the ulama and the street poets — with the towering shadow of Fuzuli over all of it. A neo-classical Arabic revival was beginning by the 1820s in poets like Abd al-Ghaffar al-Akhras. And the Baghdad singers were shaping the maqam al-Iraqi, the suite of sung classical verse that is the city's distinctive musical form.
entries.note: the 'Dīwān' of Abd al-Ghaffar al-Akhras; Scheherazade Qassim Hassan, 'Les instruments de musique en Irak' (1980), on the maqām.

entries.label: The building of the Mamluk pashas
entries.hint: The Mamluk regime, when it had money, built: Sulayman the Great and Dawud Pasha put up mosques, madrasas, khans and stretches of the covered market, in a plain Ottoman-provincial idiom of brick, dome and pointed arch. The real splendour of the period, though, went into the shrines — the domes of Kazimayn, Najaf and Karbala gilded and re-gilded with Persian and Indian money, the courtyards enlarged, the porticoes tiled.
entries.note: the Baghdad monuments in the Iraqi antiquities inventories; Sheila Blair & Jonathan Bloom, 'The Art and Architecture of Islam 1250–1800' (1994).

entries.label: Dawud Pasha's printing press
entries.hint: Among Dawud Pasha's reforms was a lithographic press, brought to Baghdad around 1821 and used to print official texts and, briefly, a small gazette — the first modern printing in Iraq. It stopped when the regime fell in 1831. The lasting presses came later, at mid-century, run by the Chaldean Church and by Jewish and government printers; but the gesture belonged to the reforming pasha.
entries.note: Wahid Gdoura, 'Le début de l'imprimerie arabe à Istanbul et en Syrie' (1985); the Iraqi press history in ʿAbd al-Razzaq al-Hilali.

entries.label: The last Mandaean scribes
entries.hint: On the lower Tigris and Euphrates the priests of the Mandaeans went on copying their scriptures — the Ginza, the Book of John — in the cursive Mandaic script, performing the river baptisms, and working as the region's goldsmiths, exactly as their forebears had for well over a millennium. European travellers described them as the last living community of a gnostic religion, and collected their manuscripts as curiosities.
entries.note: Jorunn Buckley, 'The Mandaeans: Ancient Texts and Modern People' (2002); the early accounts in Pietro della Valle and later J. H. Petermann.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The Usuli method and the rational defence of clerical authority, the Akhbari–Usuli debate and its consequences, the transmission of learning in a backwater, and the first Western science through the Residency

entries.label: The rational defence of clerical authority
entries.hint: Bihbahani's students — Bahr al-Ulum, Kashif al-Ghita, the Naraqis — worked out in detail the legal theory behind the mujtahid's power: how the qualified jurist derives rulings from the sources, why the layman is obliged to follow him, how the tithe supports him. It was a body of technical reasoning, and it turned the Najaf seminary from a school into an institution capable of acting in the world.
entries.note: Robert Gleave, 'Scripturalist Islam: The History and Doctrines of the Akhbārī Shīʿī School' (2007); Meir Litvak (1998).

entries.label: The Akhbari–Usuli debate and its stakes
entries.hint: For a century the Twelver scholars argued over method. The Akhbaris held that only the Quran and the sayings of the Imams could ground law, and denied that a living jurist had any right to reason independently or to be followed. The Usulis said reason was indispensable and the layman must emulate a living mujtahid. The Usulis won at Karbala in the late eighteenth century, and Shi'ism was set on the path toward a strong, autonomous clergy.
entries.note: Robert Gleave, 'Scripturalist Islam' (2007); Juan Cole, 'Shiʿi Clerics in Iraq and Iran' (1985).

entries.label: Transmission in the manuscript age
entries.hint: Iraqi scholarship was a receiver's culture. The Sunni ulama of Baghdad and Mosul studied a syllabus set in Istanbul and Cairo and passed on licences that tied them to Damascus and al-Azhar; the Shia studied the Najaf curriculum. Books circulated in manuscript, copied and annotated; original work was rare, careful transmission the norm. Iraq kept the tradition alive without adding much to it.
entries.note: Dina Rizk Khoury, 'State and Provincial Society' (1997), on the Mosul ulama; the ijāza networks in the biographical dictionaries.

entries.label: Science through the Residency
entries.hint: The East India Company's Residents and surgeons at Basra and Baghdad brought the first modern science: surveys of the rivers and roads, medical and weather records, and the beginnings of archaeology. Claudius Rich, Resident from 1808, measured and mapped the mounds of Babylon and Nineveh, bought cylinder seals and tablets, and published a memoir on the Babylon ruins that is reckoned the founding text of Mesopotamian archaeology.
entries.note: Claudius James Rich, 'Memoir on the Ruins of Babylon' (1815) and 'Narrative of a Residence in Koordistan' (1836, posth.); Mogens Trolle Larsen, 'The Conquest of Assyria' (1996).
